title: Resource-Efficient Bio-Molecular Docking on a NISQ-era Digital Quantum Computer
authors: Tianqi Chen, Adrian M. Mak, Jianguo Li, Jian Feng Kong, Chandra Verma, Sebastian Maurer-Stroh
abstract: Molecular docking is a vital computational task in drug discovery, wherein the objective is to efficiently identify optimal binding poses between a ligand and a target receptor protein. Due to the combinatorial explosion of possible binding configurations, docking of large and flexible molecules remains a computationally intensive problem, especially at scale. Early studies have revealed that the molecular docking can be re-cast as a maximum vertex-weighted clique problem (MVWCP) problem on a compatibility graph to be solved classically. In this work, we proposed a hybrid quantum-classical approach for molecular docking leveraging the MVWCP formalism with a variational full-basis encoding (FBE) strategy, which enables efficient encoding of classical binary variables with Bloch sphere vectors. We further prove that a global minimizer of the FBE objective can always be chosen to be a pure product state, thereby providing a rigorous justification for its optimization using a unitary variational circuit. The molecular docking problem is first mapped to a cost Hamiltonian that is minimized within a variational framework, optimized via a randomized imaginary time evolution (ITE)-inspired warm start, and gradient-based techniques. Finally, we also executed the circuit on an IBM quantum computer, underlying the feasibility and of quantum-assisted optimization for structure-based drug design and point towards the broader utility of advanced encoding techniques in quantum optimization for computational biology.
summary: This work tackles the computationally hard problem of molecular docking by reformulating it as a Maximum Vertex-Weighted Clique Problem. They introduce a hybrid quantum-classical solver utilizing a Full-Basis Encoding (FBE) strategy optimized via a warm-start procedure. The research demonstrates that FBE is a resource-efficient and rapidly converging quantum encoding for this complex optimization task on NISQ hardware.
main_problem: The paper addresses the computationally intensive molecular docking problem, which is mapped to finding a Maximum Vertex-Weighted Clique Problem (MVWCP).
main_result: They propose and demonstrate a resource-efficient hybrid quantum-classical approach using Full-Basis Encoding (FBE) that shows advantages in convergence speed over other quantum encodings.
method: The method involves mapping the problem to a cost Hamiltonian, minimizing it using a variational quantum circuit optimized via a warm-start procedure inspired by imaginary time evolution.
model_or_system: The system is molecular docking, modeled via a compatibility graph and recast as an MVWCP. The quantum computation is performed on a NISQ-era digital quantum computer (IBM quantum processor).
key_observables: Transient clique weight, raw/rounded cost functions, and single-qubit expectation values ($\langle\sigma_xangle, \langle\sigma_yangle, \langle\sigma_zangle$).
important_parameters: NISQ regime constraints, qubit connectivity, and the number of variables ($N$) in the graph problem.
main_assumptions: The global minimum of the FBE objective can be chosen to be a pure product state, justifying the use of a unitary variational circuit.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the mapping to MVWCP and the FBE strategy. Figure 7 shows MVWCP graphs for docking instances. Figure 8 compares optimization dynamics using FBE versus ZX-basis encoding.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the problem mapping (MVWCP) and the need for quantum assistance. It then details the FBE encoding and the warm-start optimization procedure. A key theoretical section proves the product state nature of the minimum, followed by comparative results showing FBE's superior convergence.
why_interesting: The rigorous mathematical proof that the global minimum is a product state provides a strong theoretical foundation for using variational quantum circuits in complex optimization tasks, which is highly relevant for quantum algorithm design.
